section.title: The Division of the Land and the City
section.sectionRationale: The book that opened with the glory of God appearing to a lone exile by a foreign river closes with all twelve tribes settled around a sanctuary at the center of the land, and a city named for nothing else but the fact that the LORD is there. This final chapter is the goal toward which the whole book, and in many ways the whole Bible, has been moving: God dwelling with His people forever.
section.thesis: The whole vision of judgment, exile, and restoration ends not in mere territory but in a name, THE LORD IS THERE, the ancient promise of God's dwelling with His people fulfilled bodily in Christ, Immanuel, God with us, and consummated forever in the new Jerusalem where God Himself dwells with man.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: the seven northern tribal portions running from Dan to Judah; the central holy district for sanctuary, priests, Levites, city, and prince; the seven southern tribal portions from Benjamin to Gad; and the city's gates, named for the twelve tribes, closing with its new name, THE LORD IS THERE.

units.label: The northern tribal portions
units.note: Dan to Judah, each bordering the next

verses.text: “Now these are the names of the tribes: At the northern frontier, Dan will have one portion bordering the road of Hethlon to Lebo-hamath and running on to Hazar-enan on the border of Damascus with Hamath to the north, and extending from the east side to the west side.
Asher will have one portion bordering the territory of Dan from east to west.
Naphtali will have one portion bordering the territory of Asher from east to west.
Manasseh will have one portion bordering the territory of Naphtali from east to west.
Ephraim will have one portion bordering the territory of Manasseh from east to west.
Reuben will have one portion bordering the territory of Ephraim from east to west.
Judah will have one portion bordering the territory of Reuben from east to west.

units.label: The central holy district
units.note: sanctuary, priests, Levites, city, and prince

verses.text: Bordering the territory of Judah, from east to west, will be the portion you are to set apart. It will be 25,000 cubits wide, and the length of a tribal portion from east to west. In the center will be the sanctuary.
The special portion you set apart to the LORD shall be 25,000 cubits long and 10,000 cubits wide.

This will be the holy portion for the priests. It will be 25,000 cubits long on the north side, 10,000 cubits wide on the west side, 10,000 cubits wide on the east side, and 25,000 cubits long on the south side. In the center will be the sanctuary of the LORD.
It will be for the consecrated priests, the descendants of Zadok, who kept My charge and did not go astray as the Levites did when the Israelites went astray.
It will be a special portion for them set apart from the land, a most holy portion adjacent to the territory of the Levites.
Bordering the territory of the priests, the Levites shall have an area 25,000 cubits long and 10,000 cubits wide. The whole length will be 25,000 cubits, and the width 10,000 cubits.
They must not sell or exchange any of it, and they must not transfer this best part of the land, for it is holy to the LORD.
The remaining area, 5,000 cubits wide and 25,000 cubits long, will be for common use by the city, for houses, and for pastureland. The city will be in the center of it
and will have these measurements: 4,500 cubits on the north side, 4,500 cubits on the south side, 4,500 cubits on the east side, and 4,500 cubits on the west side.
The pastureland of the city will extend 250 cubits to the north, 250 cubits to the south, 250 cubits to the east, and 250 cubits to the west.

The remainder of the length bordering the holy portion and running adjacent to it will be 10,000 cubits on the east side and 10,000 cubits on the west side. Its produce will supply food for the workers of the city.
The workers of the city who cultivate it will come from all the tribes of Israel.
The entire portion will be a square, 25,000 cubits by 25,000 cubits. You are to set apart the holy portion, along with the city property.

The remaining area on both sides of the holy portion and of the property of the city will belong to the {{nasi|prince}}. He will own the land adjacent to the tribal portions, extending eastward from the 25,000 cubits of the holy district toward the eastern border, and westward from the 25,000 cubits to the western border. And in the center of them will be the holy portion and the sanctuary of the temple.
So the Levitical property and the city property will lie in the center of the area belonging to the prince, the area between the borders of Judah and Benjamin.

units.label: The southern tribal portions
units.note: Benjamin to Gad, each bordering the next

verses.text: As for the rest of the tribes: Benjamin will have one portion extending from the east side to the west side.
Simeon will have one portion bordering the territory of Benjamin from east to west.
Issachar will have one portion bordering the territory of Simeon from east to west.
Zebulun will have one portion bordering the territory of Issachar from east to west.
And Gad will have one portion bordering the territory of Zebulun from east to west.
The southern border of Gad will run from Tamar to the waters of Meribath-kadesh, then along the Brook of Egypt and out to the Great Sea.
This is the land you are to allot as an inheritance to the tribes of Israel, and these will be their portions,” declares the Lord GOD.

units.label: The gates of the city: THE LORD IS THERE
units.note: Yahweh Shammah, the goal of the whole book

verses.text: “These will be the exits of the city: Beginning on the north side, which will be 4,500 cubits long,
the gates of the city will be named after the tribes of Israel. On the north side there will be three gates: the gate of Reuben, the gate of Judah, and the gate of Levi.
On the east side, which will be 4,500 cubits long, there will be three gates: the gate of Joseph, the gate of Benjamin, and the gate of Dan.
On the south side, which will be 4,500 cubits long, there will be three gates: the gate of Simeon, the gate of Issachar, and the gate of Zebulun.
And on the west side, which will be 4,500 cubits long, there will be three gates: the gate of Gad, the gate of Asher, and the gate of Naphtali.
The perimeter of the city will be 18,000 cubits, and from that day on the name of the city will be: {{yahwehShammah|THE LORD IS THERE}}.”

nasi.gloss: Prince, chief, never melek, king. His own territory here still surrounds, rather than replaces, the holy portion at the center, a final picture of authority ordered around God's presence rather than above it.

yahwehShammah.gloss: The LORD is there, Yahweh Shammah. The city's new name, and the closing word of the entire book of Ezekiel, answers every earlier scene of the glory departing with a promise that His presence will never leave again.

basic.context: This final chapter divides the whole land among the twelve tribes, seven portions running north from Dan to Judah, then the central holy district with the sanctuary, the priests' and Levites' land, the city, and the prince's own territory arranged around it, then seven more portions running south from Benjamin to Gad. The city itself gets twelve gates, three on each side, each named for a tribe, so that every tribe has a way in. And then, in the very last line of the book, the city receives its true name, not a dynasty, not a king, but a simple declaration: THE LORD IS THERE. After forty-eight chapters that began with a vision of glory by a foreign river and moved through the departure of that glory from a defiled temple, the whole book ends by answering its own deepest question. Where is God now? Right here, with His people, forever.
basic.hermeneutics: However literally or symbolically one reads the exact tribal boundaries and measurements, which even ancient interpreters recognized do not map cleanly onto the actual geography of Canaan, the chapter's climax is unmistakable and does not depend on resolving those questions: the entire, elaborate vision exists to arrive at one final sentence, a name that declares God's abiding presence with His people.
basic.originalLanguages: The nasi, prince, again never called melek, king, has his own territory arranged around, not replacing, the central sanctuary, consistent with his lay status throughout the vision. The book's final words are Yahweh Shammah, the LORD is there, a name built from the divine name itself joined to the simple adverb 'there,' making God's presence, not any human ruler or dynasty, the city's entire identity.
basic.typology: The city named for God's presence anticipates the Word becoming flesh and tabernacling among us, John 1:14, God's presence no longer symbolized by a name over a city but embodied in a person. The twelve gates, named for the twelve tribes so that every tribe has access, anticipate the twelve gates of the new Jerusalem, named for the twelve tribes of Israel, in Revelation 21:12-13, opened now to people from every nation.
basic.christ: Isaiah had already promised that a virgin would conceive and bear a son, and they will call Him Immanuel, meaning, 'God with us,' Matthew 1:23, the fulfillment in a person of what Ezekiel 48:35 promises in a place. Revelation 21:2-3 shows the new Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, and a loud voice from the throne declaring, 'Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them, and they will be His people, and God Himself will be with them,' the very promise, THE LORD IS THERE, made permanent and unshakable, this time never again to be threatened by departure.
basic.god: God's whole purpose across this long and difficult book has been to dwell with His people, not to abandon them; the glory left in judgment in chapters 8-11 precisely so that it could return in undiminished mercy here, and the entire elaborate ordering of tribes, priesthood, and city exists only to make room for, and to name, His abiding presence.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 25:8 first states God's intention that Israel build Him a sanctuary so that I may dwell among them. Matthew 1:23 identifies Jesus as Immanuel, God with us, fulfilling the promise of this city's name in a person. Revelation 21:3 declares that the dwelling place of God is with man forever. Revelation 21:12-13 shows the new Jerusalem's twelve gates named for the twelve tribes of Israel, echoing Ezekiel 48:31-34.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible can be read as the story of a God who made a good world to dwell with His people, lost that dwelling through sin, and has been working ever since, through tabernacle, temple, exile, and promised return, to dwell with them again. Ezekiel's vision, from the glory departing in judgment to that same glory returning to fill a new temple and finally to name an entire city THE LORD IS THERE, traces the whole arc of that story. It reaches its center in Jesus Christ, Immanuel, God with us in flesh and blood, and its final, unshakable fulfillment in Revelation 21, where God's dwelling place is with man forever, and the need for any temple at all disappears, because the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.

context.literary:
Chapter 48 is a carefully built map in words, and its design is the message. The chapter has a symmetrical frame: seven tribal bands in the north, verses 1 to 7, then the central district, verses 8 to 22, then five bands in the south, verses 23 to 27, and finally the city's gates, verses 30 to 35. The two lists of tribes are told with almost the same sentence repeated, 'one portion bordering the territory of' the last tribe 'from east to west'. The repetition produces a feeling of rule and order: each tribe has the same kind of share, a strip running across the whole land.

At the centre everything is arranged around the sanctuary. The phrase 'in the center' keeps returning, verses 8, 10 and 15, and the holy district is described again and again in nested rectangles: priests, Levites, then city, then the prince on both sides. The prince's land is the frame of the frame, flanking the holy district, verses 21 to 22, so that the ruler sits at the edges and the sanctuary at the heart.

The final unit, verses 30 to 35, turns from land to city and ends with a name. The perimeter is measured, three gates are set on each side, and the last line of the book gives the city's new name. After forty-eight chapters of measurement, the measurements end with a declaration of presence. The book that opened with the glory of the LORD arriving from the north, 1:4, in exile, closes with a place named for His staying.

The chapter also completes a design begun in chapter 47. The borders in 47:15 to 20 are repeated in part, with the southern line from Tamar to Meribath-kadesh and the Brook of Egypt, 48:28, so that the long speech about land is framed by the same edges at its beginning and end.
context.historical:
The tribal order has its own history. The twelve strips run straight across the land from the Jordan to the Mediterranean, one above another, a pattern that does not match Joshua's allotments, in which the tribes took irregular regions and some sat east of the Jordan. Dan, which had in fact moved to the far north in the book of Judges, takes the very top. Judah and Benjamin, the two tribes that stayed with David's house and Jerusalem, are placed on either side of the holy district, so that the strip that held the old capital is now the neighbour of the sanctuary.

The tribes of Jacob's two maidservants' sons, Dan, Naphtali, Asher and Gad, are given the outermost positions, three in the far north and one in the far south. Leah's and Rachel's sons are nearer the centre. Yet all twelve strips are of the same kind, and each tribe has a gate. In the exile the northern tribes had been gone for more than a century, since the fall of Samaria, and many of the people who heard Ezekiel were from Judah. The vision restores all twelve.

The city is a modest place. It is a square of 4,500 cubits on a side, about a mile and a half, with an open margin of 250 cubits. It does not sit in the holy district but in the common strip beside it, 48:15, so it is not Zion in the old sense. It is a working place with fields whose workers come from all the tribes, verses 18 to 19. The old Jerusalem had been a royal city with a Temple within its walls, and this one has the Temple at one remove.
context.canonical:
The name of the city belongs to a family of names. Jerusalem is to be called 'The Throne of the LORD', Jeremiah 3:17, and 'The LORD Our Righteousness', Jeremiah 33:16, and Isaiah promises 'a new name that the mouth of the LORD will bestow', Isaiah 62:2, so that the city shall be called 'Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken', Isaiah 62:12. Earlier in Ezekiel, God had said of Edom's boast that it would possess the land, 'even though the LORD was there', 35:10, and had said that He would be 'a sanctuary' for the exiles for a little while, 11:16. The final verse gives the place its permanent name.

The twelve gates return in the New Testament. The new Jerusalem has 'twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel', three on each side, Revelation 21:12 to 13, and its measurement is a square, Revelation 21:16. The fact that John sees 'no temple in the city', 21:22, takes Ezekiel's pattern a step further: where Ezekiel names the city for God's presence, John says God Himself is the temple.

The theme of God dwelling with His people runs from Exodus 25:8 and Leviticus 26:11 to 12 to John 1:14, Matthew 1:23 and Revelation 21:3. And the equal shares of the land are carried over into the New Testament's promise that the meek will inherit the earth, Matthew 5:5, and that those in Christ are heirs together, Galatians 3:29.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel meant his hearers to find in the closing chapter the answer to the question that had haunted the book, whether God had left them for good. The long section on measurements, borders and portions is a way of saying that the future is not a vague hope but a place with edges, a city with a gate for every tribe and a God in the middle. The details are a form of assurance. A prophet does not draw a map for a people he expects to be forgotten.

The equal bands carry a moral intention. Every tribe, including the ones that had been lost for a century, receives a strip of the same form, and no one is farther from the sanctuary in any way that matters, since the holy portion runs the whole breadth of the land. The names on the gates say that no tribe has to enter by another's door.

The last words are the intention of the whole book in one phrase. Ezekiel began in a foreign land seeing glory he could not explain and ends with a name that explains it: the LORD is there.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is told in the future tense and in the form of a land survey, but it is a vision and not a decree for the exiles' return. The returned community under Zerubbabel and Nehemiah did not divide the land this way, which shows that Israel did not take it as an immediate command. The chapter is also not a modern political programme. No state or church may take its measurements as a blueprint.

What the church draws from it is the substance. God's people live around His presence, the leader is not set above the people, the weak and the despised are given a full share, and the worship of God sits at the middle of the shared life, not at the edge. The close of the chapter teaches believers to read their own city of residence in the light of a better one, as Hebrews 13:14 says: 'we are looking for the city that is to come.'

debates.question: Do the tribal boundaries describe a future literal division of the land?

views.label: A literal future allotment
views.case: Some read the strips, the holy district and the city as a plan for a restored Israel in the last days, with the temple of chapters 40 to 43 rebuilt in the middle. They point to the detailed dimensions and the use of real place names as signs that a real land is in view.

views.label: A symbolic picture of complete and equal belonging
views.case: Others observe that parallel bands running straight across the land do not follow the real hills, valleys and coast. They take the design as an ideal picture of order, in which each tribe is equally near God, with its fulfilment in the new Jerusalem and its twelve gates, Revelation 21:12 to 13.

debates.bearing: Both agree the chapter's centre is the God who dwells in the middle. The New Testament adds that the people around that centre are drawn from every nation, so the picture is already being filled out in Christ.

debates.question: What is the relation of the city to the sanctuary?

views.label: The city is the sanctuary's holy dwelling
views.case: Because the city takes its name from the presence of the LORD, some read the whole city as a holy place, so that God's presence has spread beyond the temple court to the city. This agrees with Jeremiah 3:17, where the city is called 'The Throne of the LORD'.

views.label: The city is common land beside the holy
views.case: The text calls the city's land 'common', verse 15, and places it in a strip beside the holy district, verses 15 to 20. On this reading the city is an ordinary place of homes and farms, and its name says that the LORD is present even where there is no sacred fence.

debates.bearing: The name is the same on either reading: God is in the middle of His people, and holiness reaches to the common. That fits Zechariah 14:20 to 21, where ordinary pots are holy.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's repeated word for the tribal strip is chelqah echad, 'one portion', and the language of equal shares is stressed by the fact that every tribe is told the same thing. The root chalaq means 'to divide, to share out'. It is related to cheleq, the 'portion' that the LORD was to the priests in Numbers 18:20. So when Ezekiel says the land is divided into portions, the word reminds the reader that God's own portion is the centre.

The central district is a terumah, 'a special portion', verses 8, 9 and 10, a root meaning 'to lift up', as the portion is lifted off the land and set apart. In verse 12 the priests' part is called qodesh qodashim, 'most holy', the same phrase that names the inner room of the Temple. The BSB footnote says the Hebrew may also be read 'a Most Holy Place', so even the land of the priests takes on the quality of the innermost room. The district is set apart because it is lifted up, and the lifting is the first act of giving.

The land of the Levites 'must not be sold or exchanged', verse 14, because it is 'the best part of the land', reshit ha'arets. The word reshit means 'first' or 'beginning' and is the word of Genesis 1:1 and of the firstfruits, as in Proverbs 3:9. The best of the land is the part given to the LORD's servants. It is the opposite of the grasping that the prophets had condemned in 45:8 to 9.

The city's land is called chol, 'common', in verse 15, the same word that the priests were told to distinguish from the holy in 44:23. The city is therefore not sacred territory but a normal place, and it is surrounded by a migrash, 'pastureland', verses 15 and 17, the word that Joshua 21 uses for the grazing land around the Levitical cities. The city is a town like the others, with grazing lands for its animals.

The gates are named for 'exits', totsa'ot, from the verb yatsa, 'to go out', in verse 30. The city is described by how people leave it as well as how they enter. Finally, the name in verse 35 is Yahweh Shammah, in which shammah is the adverb 'there'. It is a compound name of the same kind as 'The LORD Will Provide', Genesis 22:14, 'The LORD Is My Banner', Exodus 17:15, and 'The LORD Is Peace', Judges 6:24: a place or an altar named for what God has shown Himself to be there.

typology.type: The central holy district with the city around the sanctuary, 48:8 to 20
typology.fulfillment: Everything in the chapter is arranged around a center where God dwells. In Christ that center is a Person: 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us', John 1:14, and 'in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form', Colossians 2:9. The church is built around Him as the cornerstone and grows into a holy temple, Ephesians 2:20 to 22. The correspondence is the placing of God's presence at the middle of His people; the escalation is that the center is now a living Person and also a people, 1 Corinthians 3:16. The type falls short because the district is still a fenced space.

typology.type: The twelve gates named for the tribes, 48:30 to 34
typology.fulfillment: Each tribe has a gate, three to a side, and each gate bears a tribal name. Revelation 21:12 to 13 sees the same arrangement, twelve gates with the names of the tribes and three on each side. The wall of the city also has twelve foundations bearing the names of the apostles, Revelation 21:14, so the people of both covenants are in one city. The correspondence is open access for all the tribes; the escalation is that Jesus calls Himself 'the gate', John 10:9, and the nations come in through the gates, Revelation 21:24 to 26. The type is incomplete without the nations.

typology.type: The city renamed THE LORD IS THERE, 48:35
typology.fulfillment: The name declares the permanent presence of God. In Jesus the prophecy 'they will call Him Immanuel' is given the meaning 'God with us', Matthew 1:23, and He promises 'I am with you always, even to the end of the age', Matthew 28:20, and 'where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them', Matthew 18:20. In the end 'the dwelling place of God is with man', Revelation 21:3. The type falls short only in being a name over a place, where the New Testament names a Person and a people.

typology.type: The equal portions of every tribe, 48:1 to 7 and 48:23 to 29
typology.fulfillment: The twelve strips of equal form picture a people in which no group is shut out of the inheritance. Paul writes that in Christ 'there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female', Galatians 3:28, and 'if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise', Galatians 3:29. Jesus says the meek will inherit the earth, Matthew 5:5. The correspondence is fairness in the shared inheritance; the escalation is that the inheritance becomes the whole new creation, Romans 4:13 and Revelation 21:7.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by its name. The city is called THE LORD IS THERE, and the New Testament tells how that came true. 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us', John 1:14, and the verb 'dwelling' is the old tabernacle verb. At His birth the angel's word is that they will call Him Immanuel, 'God with us', Matthew 1:23. At His departure He says, 'I am with you always, even to the end of the age', Matthew 28:20. Ezekiel's long absence of glory, the departure in chapters 10 and 11, is answered in a Man in whom God Himself has come to stay. Paul says that all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell in Him, Colossians 1:19.

The gates lead to Christ through the way in which every tribe gets a gate. Jesus says 'I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved', John 10:9. The twelve tribes' gates are given in Revelation 21:12 to 13, and the Lamb is the lamp of that city, Revelation 21:23. The arrangement means all of God's people enter by one name and through one Saviour. The twelve foundations carrying the apostles' names, Revelation 21:14, show that the city rests on the One they proclaimed.

The equal inheritance leads to Christ in Galatians 3:29, 'if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise', and in Ephesians 3:6, where Gentiles are 'fellow heirs'. What the exiles hoped for as a division of land, the New Testament calls a share in 'an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading', 1 Peter 1:4, kept in Christ.

The prince's place on the edge of the holy district also bears on Christ. The Davidic ruler in Ezekiel lives beside the sanctuary and does not occupy it. The Son of David is not content with the edge. He is the true Temple, John 2:19 to 21, and also the ruler who has been given all authority, Matthew 28:18.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The arithmetic of 4,500 and 25,000 cubits, the order of the tribes and the placing of Dan are not coded descriptions of Christ's life. What the New Testament takes up is the central presence, the open gates, the equal heirs and the name, and it reads them as fulfilled in Christ and consummated in the new creation.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God whose final self-disclosure is presence. After a book of judgment, visions of throne chariots, glory leaving the Temple and measurements of a new house, the last thing said is the name of the city: THE LORD IS THERE. The God of Ezekiel is not remembered mainly as a God who judged but as the God who stays. He is the One who told the exiles in 11:16 that He would be a sanctuary to them for a little while, and who now says that the little while has become permanent.

He is a God of order. Every tribe has its place, every measure is exact, and every part of the plan has been given a position around Him. His order is not cold. The land is divided so that no tribe is lost, the priests and Levites are provided for, the city has its workers and fields, and the prince has land of his own so that he does not need to take any, 45:8. The order protects the weak.

He is faithful to His oath. The same boundaries He swore to give to the forefathers, 47:14, are repeated, and the lists of the tribes include the ones the world had written off. He is the God who says 'all twelve', and that is a sign that the promise to Abraham is not cancelled by exile. His faithfulness does not depend on Israel's record.

He is a God who is at the center and who also dwells among the common. The city is called common, yet it bears the name that says He is there. His holiness does not exclude ordinary life; it enters it. Zechariah 14:20 to 21 pictures that same truth with cooking pots.

He is also a God who gives names. He names the city, as He named Abram and Jacob and as He will give His people a new name, Isaiah 62:2. A name given by God is a promise about what a place will be, and He fulfils it.

For worship, the chapter calls us to trust that the God who has gone away from our failures has also come back and means to stay. We are to rejoice in the nearness of a God who said, 'I will walk among you and be your God', Leviticus 26:12, and to sing, as Psalm 46:5 does, that God is within the city.

crossReferences.note: God commands 'And they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them.' This is the first statement of the purpose of the tabernacle, and the last verse of Ezekiel brings it to a close. The place is named for the dwelling itself, so the long arc from the tabernacle to the city is one story.

In the exile God said He had been 'a sanctuary for them in the countries to which they have gone' for a little while. Ezekiel 48:35 is the other end of that phrase: the little while is over and the city bears the name of a presence that is no longer temporary.

Edom boasted that it would possess the land 'even though the LORD was there'. The phrase uses the same idea of the LORD's presence in the land that is crowned in the last verse of the book. Edom's boast was made against a God who was in fact present.

Jerusalem is to be called 'The LORD Our Righteousness' in the days of the righteous Branch. Like Ezekiel 48:35, the name of the city carries a statement about the LORD, and both promise that the restored city will be known for who God is rather than for who the people are.

The people will be called 'the Holy People, the Redeemed of The LORD', and the city 'Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken'. Isaiah and Ezekiel both end with names, and both reverse the language of abandonment that the exile had taught.

God promises to make His dwelling among His people and to walk among them, so that He will be their God and they His people. The covenant formula behind Ezekiel 48:35 is here: the presence of God is the heart of the covenant, and the city's name is its fullest statement.

The virgin's son will be called Immanuel, 'God with us'. The name of Ezekiel's city, THE LORD IS THERE, becomes a person in the Gospel, and Matthew places it at the beginning of the New Testament as the meaning of Jesus.

The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. The verb of dwelling recalls the tabernacle, and John says that the glory that left Ezekiel's Temple has been seen in Jesus, full of grace and truth.

The new Jerusalem has twelve gates inscribed with the names of the tribes of Israel, three on each side. John sees what Ezekiel 48:31 to 34 describes, with its twelve gates and four sides, which makes this the clearest New Testament use of the chapter.

A voice from the throne says that the dwelling place of God is with man and that He will dwell with them. The sentence is the New Testament's reading of Ezekiel's closing name and makes the presence the permanent condition of the redeemed.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with God walking in a garden with His creatures, Genesis 3:8, and the loss of that nearness is the first wound of the Bible. The garden is closed, the cherubim are posted, and from then on the story is a long effort to get back to a place where God is with His people. The tabernacle, the Temple, the cloud and the glory are all steps toward that end. Ezekiel 48 puts the last words of that long effort in a name.

The chapter answers what came before it. The glory had left the Temple in chapters 10 and 11, and the exiles had asked whether God was gone. Chapter 43 had brought the glory back. Now the whole land and city are arranged around it, and the city is called by a name that says He will not go again. It also answers the failure of Israel, for the land that was lost through unfaithfulness is given again by grace, with a share for every tribe.

The chapter sets up the New Testament in two ways. First, it prepares the claim that God has come to dwell in a person, Immanuel, John 1:14 and Matthew 1:23. Second, it prepares the new Jerusalem. Revelation 21 describes a city of twelve gates, named for the twelve tribes, built as a square, with the glory of God as its light, Revelation 21:23. John adds that he saw no temple in it, because God and the Lamb are its temple, 21:22. What Ezekiel's name promised has no need of a building.

The story ends with the voice from the throne: 'Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God', Revelation 21:3. The garden's loss is reversed and the city carries Ezekiel's name in its fullness. The last chapter of the Bible adds that the river of life flows through its street, and that God's servants 'will see His face', Revelation 22:1 to 4, which is where the long journey ends.

quiz.q: How many tribal portions run north of the central holy district, from Dan to Judah?

options.text: Seven, Dan, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, Reuben, and Judah
options.note: 48:1-7 lists exactly these seven tribes running north to south down to the holy district.

options.text: Twelve, including every tribe in a single northern band
options.note: The twelve tribes are split, seven north and five south, of the central district.

options.text: Three, matching the three gates on each side of the city
options.note: The gate count of three per side is separate from the seven northern tribal portions.

options.text: Five, with the rest placed south of the holy district
options.note: Seven tribes are placed north; five, Benjamin through Gad, are placed south, 48:23-27.

quiz.q: Where is the prince's own territory located relative to the holy district and the city?

options.text: On both sides of the holy portion and the city property, bordering the tribal portions
options.note: 48:21 places the prince's land flanking the central district on the east and west.

options.text: Inside the sanctuary grounds themselves, alongside the priests
options.note: The sanctuary and priestly land are explicitly distinct from, and holier than, the prince's surrounding territory.

options.text: Entirely outside the boundaries of the land altogether
options.note: His territory is explicitly within the land, adjacent to the holy district.

options.text: Replacing the Levites' portion after their earlier demotion
options.note: The Levites retain their own distinct portion, 48:13-14; the prince's land is separate from theirs.

quiz.q: How are the city's twelve gates arranged and named?

options.text: Three gates on each of the four sides, each gate named after one of the twelve tribes of Israel
options.note: 48:31-34 lists three gates per side, twelve total, each bearing a tribal name.

options.text: One gate for each cardinal direction, named for the four largest tribes only
options.note: There are twelve gates total, three per side, not merely four gates for four tribes.

options.text: Twelve gates, but left unnamed to avoid tribal favoritism
options.note: Each gate is explicitly named for a specific tribe, 48:31-34.

options.text: Gates named only for Levi, Joseph, and Judah, repeated on every side
options.note: All twelve tribes receive a distinct named gate, not merely these three repeated.

quiz.q: What is the new name given to the city in the final verse of the book, 48:35?

options.text: THE LORD IS THERE
options.note: 48:35 gives this exact name, Yahweh Shammah, as the closing statement of the entire book.

options.text: The City of David, restored
options.note: This traditional name for Jerusalem is not the name given in this verse.

options.text: The city receives no new name; it keeps its former name
options.note: The text explicitly states a new name is given, effective from that day forward.

options.text: The Holy Sanctuary of Zadok
options.note: The name given centers on the LORD's presence, not on the priestly line of Zadok.

quiz.q: How does Revelation 21:3 fulfill the promise named in Ezekiel 48:35?

options.text: A loud voice from the throne declares that the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them forever, the same promise made permanent and unshakable
options.note: Revelation 21:3 states this directly, completing what Ezekiel 48:35 names in the city, THE LORD IS THERE.

options.text: It declares that God's presence will again depart, as it did in Ezekiel 8-11
options.note: Revelation 21 describes the opposite, an unending, unshakable dwelling of God with man.

options.text: It limits God's dwelling to a rebuilt physical temple structure alone
options.note: Revelation 21:22 explicitly says no temple is needed, since God and the Lamb are its temple.

options.text: It restricts this promise only to the twelve tribes of Israel by blood
options.note: Revelation 21 broadens this dwelling to the nations, whose glory is brought into the city, Revelation 21:24-26.

questions: The whole elaborate ordering of tribes, priesthood, and prince exists only to arrive at one final name, THE LORD IS THERE. What in your own life is ultimately for the sake of God's presence, rather than an end in itself, once you strip away the details?

Every tribe, without exception, gets its own named gate into the city. Is there a part of your own story or identity you have assumed has no place near God's presence, that this picture of complete, named belonging might correct?

The prince's own territory is arranged around, not replacing, the sanctuary at the center. Where might you need to reorder your own priorities so that God's presence, not your own position or comfort, sits at the center?
Jesus is named Immanuel, God with us, the personal fulfillment of this city's name. How does it change your prayer life this week to remember that God is not distant but literally with you in Christ?
Revelation 21 promises that God's dwelling with His people will never again be threatened by departure. What fear or instability in your own life might this unshakable promise be meant to steady?
